title: Topological Boundary States and the Edge Chain in Semi-Infinite Two-Dimensional Insulators
authors: Ilya Iakoub, Nicolas Levasseur, Richard MacKenzie
abstract: We show that it is possible to compute the adiabatically protected edge and corner states of semi-infinite, two-dimensional, topological insulators by considering the first layer of lattice sites, what we call the "edge chain," independently from the bulk. We start by accepting this claim as an ansatz, then, using the Shemesh theorem, we show that the edge states one finds using our procedure are adiabatically protected, provided we restrict ourselves to adiabatic evolutions that do not break chiral symmetry. We show explicit examples of our method in a 2D extension of the SSH model, the SSH3 model, the Haldane model and the Breathing Kagome Lattice.
summary: This paper introduces a powerful 'edge chain' method to calculate the topologically protected edge and corner states in 2D topological insulators. By treating the boundary layer independently, the authors demonstrate that these states can be found using advanced mathematical tools applied to the analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian. This provides a systematic approach for analyzing boundary physics in complex quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the adiabatically protected edge and corner states in semi-infinite, two-dimensional topological insulators.
main_result: A novel 'edge chain' method is proposed, which successfully computes these boundary states by analyzing only the first layer of lattice sites, and the protection of these states is confirmed using Shemesh's theorem.
method: The method involves analytically continuing the Bloch Hamiltonian to the complex plane, treating the boundary as an independent 'edge chain,' and applying conditions derived from the bulk structure.
model_or_system: The study focuses on semi-infinite 2D topological insulators, using extensions of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, the Haldane model, and the Breathing Kagome Lattice as explicit examples.
key_observables: Edge and corner state wave functions, energy eigenvalues, and the dimension of the kernel space defining the boundary states.
important_parameters: Chiral symmetry, the complex wave number $z$, and the hopping parameters ($t_1, t_2, t_3$) defining the lattice structure.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that edge states can be found by considering only the first layer ('edge chain') independently of the bulk, and that the connecting sites can be set to zero amplitude.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 2D SSH model, labeling the 'edge chain' sites, and show visualizations of the model with alternative unit cells used to find different types of boundary states.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the edge chain ansatz, using Shemesh's theorem to prove protection, and then applying this framework to specific models (SSH3, Haldane, Kagome) using advanced techniques like para-Hermiticity and analyzing exceptional points.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed for finding boundary states in non-Hermitian, quasi-periodic systems is highly relevant to understanding topological phases in open quantum systems or engineered photonic/acoustic lattices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: 2D extension of the SSH model. The full lines are t1 hoppings, the dashed lines are t2 hoppings. In the shaded area, you have the unit cell we use. On the right, we show the labeling of the edge chain sites.
FIG. 2: To enforce the edge chain ansatz, we set every second “chain” to zero. The resulting wave function is shown above. The white circles represent sites where the wave function amplitude is zero.

FIG. 3: The 2D SSH model with another unit cell, identified by a shaded area in the image on the left. On the right, we show the corresponding ansatz. The white circles represent sites where the wave function amplitude is zero.

FIG. 4: (Color online). In orange: sites with amplitude ψi; in green sites with amplitude ψb. When a Bloch state satisfies the boundary condition, ψb = 0. On the left: the ψi and ψb for the unit cell in Fig. 1; on the right: for the unit cell in Fig. 3.

FIG. 5: A possible trajectory of the point z0, where an eigenstate of h2(z) is shared with h1(z), generated by the transformations U(z, t). If the shared state happens to arise at an exceptional point of h2(z), there will be a band crossing along z0(t), which translates into a gap closing when |z0(t)| = 1.
